p.src: Now Cai Jing made inquiries at the Imperial Military Academy about the official who had refused to listen to his discourse on warfare and had instead stared up at a corner of the roof. His surname was Luo, his given name Jian; his ancestral home was in Dazhou of the Yunnan Commandery, and he was then serving as an instructor at the academy. Cai Jing's breast filled with anger, and he was just about to vent it when word came that the emperor's carriage had arrived. He therefore let the matter drop, led the assembled officials out to welcome His Majesty into the academy, and, after bowing and dancing in homage, cried long life three times. When the Daojun Emperor had finished reviewing the martial exercises, Luo Jian, the academy instructor, stepped forward and prostrated himself before Cai Jing could speak, memorializing first: “I, your insignificant servant Luo Jian, an instructor at the Imperial Military Academy, venture at the risk of ten thousand deaths to report for Your Majesty's hearing the circumstances of the powerful rebel Wang Qing's revolt in Huaixi. Wang Qing has been in rebellion in Huaixi for five years now, and the imperial forces have been unable to withstand him. Tong Guan and Cai You went by imperial command to campaign in Huaixi, only to lose their entire army. Fearing punishment, they concealed the truth and deceived Your Majesty, claiming that the soldiers could not endure the climate and proposing that the campaign be suspended for the time being, thereby allowing this grave menace to grow. Wang Qing has grown ever more rampant. Last month he even captured my native Yun'an Commandery, where his men plundered, violated women, and slaughtered the people with cruelties too dreadful to relate. Altogether he now occupies eight prefectural commands and eighty-six prefectures and counties. Cai Jing bears the weighty charge of assisting the sovereign, while his son Cai You has lost armies and generals in this fashion, disgracing the realm and destroying its forces. Yet before Your Majesty arrived today, Cai Jing still sat grandly in the place of honor discoursing on war, shamelessly boasting—mad and bereft of reason! I beg Your Majesty swiftly to execute Cai Jing and the other traitorous ministers who have brought ruin upon the state, choose commanders, muster troops, and promptly launch a campaign of suppression, rescuing the people from misery and disaster and preserving the dynasty for boundless ages. Great will be the good fortune of Your Majesty's subjects! Great will be the good fortune of all under Heaven!” The Daojun Emperor was furious when he heard the memorial and sternly rebuked Cai Jing and the others for concealing the matter. But Cai Jing and his associates artfully talked the emperor around, so he did not punish them at once, but ordered his carriage and returned to the palace.

p.src: The next day, Hou Meng, prefect of Bozhou, arrived in the capital to await assignment and submitted a forthright memorial accusing Tong Guan and Cai You of losing the army and disgracing the nation. He also recommended: “Song Jiang and his companions possess extraordinary ability and strategy and have repeatedly accomplished remarkable feats. After returning from the campaign against Liao, they pacified Hebei as well, and have now reported victory and begun their triumphal return. Wang Qing is now running rampant. I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict, first rewarding and commending Song Jiang and his companions, and then ordering this army to campaign in Huaixi. They will assuredly achieve a great victory.” Emperor Huizong approved the memorial and immediately sent an edict to the Secretariat and the Bureau, ordering them to deliberate upon ranks and titles for Song Jiang and the others. After consulting Cai Jing and his associates, the officials of the Secretariat and the Bureau reported: “Wang Qing has captured Wanzhou, and only yesterday urgent dispatches arrived from Yuzhou, Zaizhou, and Lai County requesting aid. Those three places are prefectures and counties under the Eastern Capital and lie close to the imperial capital. We beg Your Majesty to command Chen Guan, Song Jiang, and the others not to return to the capital, but to lead their forces with all speed, day and night, to the relief of Yuzhou and the other threatened places. We recommend Hou Meng as staff adviser to the expeditionary army. Luo Jian has long been versed in strategy; let him accompany Hou Meng and report to Chen Guan's army for service. As Song Jiang and the others are presently engaged in a campaign, it would be inconvenient to promote and invest them now. When they report victory in Huaixi, their rewards and titles may be separately considered.” In truth, Cai Jing knew that Wang Qing had powerful troops and fierce commanders. After conferring with Tong Guan, Yang Jian, and Gao Qiu, he deliberately arranged for Hou Meng and Luo Jian to be sent to Chen Guan. Once Song Jiang and the others were defeated, where could Hou Meng and Luo Jian flee—even if they could ascend to Heaven? Would they not then all be swept into the same net? But let us not burden the tale with needless detail. The four traitorous ministers submitted their proposal, and the Daojun Emperor approved every point. He issued an edict and at once ordered Hou Meng and Luo Jian to bear the imperial rescript and take charge of the rewards—gold and silver, bolts of satin, robes, armor, horses, imperial wine, and other articles. They were to depart that very day, hasten to Hebei, and proclaim the imperial command to Song Jiang and the others. The responsible ministry was further ordered promptly to recommend and appoint principal and assistant officials to all vacant posts in the newly recovered prefectures and counties of Hebei, setting them a strict deadline to hasten to their offices. When the Daojun Emperor had finished deciding these matters, Wang Fu and Cai You once more persuaded him to go and amuse himself at Genyue. Of that no more need be said.

p.src: The decree declared: We revere Heaven and follow Our ancestors, continuing the succession to the great imperial foundation, and rely upon outstanding and able pillars of state to assist Us in the great enterprise. Of late there have been frequent alarms on the frontiers, and the fortunes of the realm have known little peace. You, Vanguard Commissioner Song Jiang and your companions, have traversed mountains and rivers and crossed perilous obstacles, first accomplishing the pacification of the northern enemy and then reporting success in quelling the bandits. We have indeed been pleased to rely upon you. We now specially dispatch Staff Adviser Hou Meng to bear this edict and bestow upon Pacification Commissioner Chen Guan, Song Jiang, Lu Junyi, and the others gold and silver, robes and satin, fine horses, clothing and armor, imperial wine, and other articles, thereby making manifest your achievements. Now the powerful rebel Wang Qing has again risen in revolt in Huaixi, overthrowing Our cities, slaughtering Our people, ravaging Our borderlands, and shaking Our Western Capital. We therefore retain Chen Guan as pacification commissioner and appoint Song Jiang chief vanguard for the pacification of the west, Lu Junyi deputy vanguard for the pacification of the west, and Hou Meng staff adviser to the expeditionary army. On the day this edict arrives, you shall immediately command your forces and hasten with all speed first to the relief of Wanzhou. p.src: Reader, keep the thread of the tale firmly in mind and listen closely, while we relate the story of Wang Qing from childhood to manhood. Wang Qing had originally been a deputy infantry officer in the Kaifeng Prefecture of the Eastern Capital. His father, Wang Xi, was a wealthy man of the Eastern Capital who made a specialty of manipulating the government offices. He instigated lawsuits, encouraged vexatious litigation, played every kind of rogue’s trick, and framed decent people; for this reason, everyone yielded him some ground. He trusted the word of a geomancer who had found a burial site that was supposed to produce a son of the highest distinction. The land was already the burial ground of one of Wang Xi’s relatives, so Wang Xi and the geomancer devised a scheme to ruin that family. Wang Xi came forward as the chief accuser and lodged a false complaint against them. The lawsuit dragged on for years until their property was exhausted. Unable to contend with Wang Xi, the family left the Eastern Capital and settled far away. Later, when Wang Qing rebelled and all three branches of his clan were exterminated, this family alone survived because they lived far away and the authorities discovered that they had been victims of Wang Xi. Wang Xi seized the burial ground and interred his parents there. In due course, his wife became pregnant and reached full term. Wang Xi dreamed that a tiger entered his house and crouched in the western part of the hall, whereupon a lion-like beast suddenly burst in, seized the tiger in its jaws, and carried it away. When Wang Xi awoke, his wife gave birth to Wang Qing. Wang Qing was wild and dissolute from childhood. By the age of sixteen or seventeen he had grown powerfully built and immensely strong. Instead of studying, he delighted in cockfighting, horse racing, wielding spears, and swinging staves. Wang Xi and his wife had no child but Wang Qing and doted on him excessively. They always shielded his faults and let him have his way, so once he was grown, how could they possibly restrain him? His pursuits were gambling away his money, sleeping with prostitutes, and drinking wine. Wang Xi and his wife did admonish him from time to time. But whenever Wang Qing’s perverse temper flared, he cursed his parents. Wang Xi was helpless and could only let him do as he pleased. After six or seven years, Wang Qing had squandered the entire family fortune. With nothing but his own prowess to depend upon, he took a post as a deputy infantry officer in the prefecture. Whenever he had money in hand, he gathered his sworn brothers around him and feasted all day on wine and meat; but at the slightest displeasure, out came his fists. Thus everyone both feared and liked him.

u.src: Wang Qing had originally been a deputy infantry officer in the Kaifeng Prefecture of the Eastern Capital.

His father, Wang Xi, was a wealthy man of the Eastern Capital who made a specialty of manipulating the government offices. He instigated lawsuits, encouraged vexatious litigation, played every kind of rogue’s trick, and framed decent people; for this reason, everyone yielded him some ground.
He trusted the word of a geomancer who had found a burial site that was supposed to produce a son of the highest distinction.
The land was already the burial ground of one of Wang Xi’s relatives, so Wang Xi and the geomancer devised a scheme to ruin that family.

Wang Xi came forward as the chief accuser and lodged a false complaint against them. The lawsuit dragged on for years until their property was exhausted. Unable to contend with Wang Xi, the family left the Eastern Capital and settled far away.

Later, when Wang Qing rebelled and all three branches of his clan were exterminated, this family alone survived because they lived far away and the authorities discovered that they had been victims of Wang Xi.
Wang Xi seized the burial ground and interred his parents there. In due course, his wife became pregnant and reached full term.
Wang Xi dreamed that a tiger entered his house and crouched in the western part of the hall, whereupon a lion-like beast suddenly burst in, seized the tiger in its jaws, and carried it away.
When Wang Xi awoke, his wife gave birth to Wang Qing.

Wang Qing was wild and dissolute from childhood. By the age of sixteen or seventeen he had grown powerfully built and immensely strong. Instead of studying, he delighted in cockfighting, horse racing, wielding spears, and swinging staves.
Wang Xi and his wife had no child but Wang Qing and doted on him excessively. They always shielded his faults and let him have his way, so once he was grown, how could they possibly restrain him?
His pursuits were gambling away his money, sleeping with prostitutes, and drinking wine.
Wang Xi and his wife did admonish him from time to time.
But whenever Wang Qing’s perverse temper flared, he cursed his parents.
Wang Xi was helpless and could only let him do as he pleased.
After six or seven years, Wang Qing had squandered the entire family fortune. With nothing but his own prowess to depend upon, he took a post as a deputy infantry officer in the prefecture.
Whenever he had money in hand, he gathered his sworn brothers around him and feasted all day on wine and meat; but at the slightest displeasure, out came his fists.
Thus everyone both feared and liked him.

p.src: One day, Wang Qing entered the government office at the fifth watch to answer the morning roll call. When his duties were done, he strolled out through the southern gate and went sightseeing in the Yujin Gardens. This was in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era under Emperor Huizong. It was mid-spring. Sightseers swarmed like ants and mounted soldiers massed like clouds. Just so: In the imperial gardens flowers bloom and willows doze beside the dikes; among the throngs of pleasure-seekers mingle lovely women. Horses with golden bridles neigh upon the fragrant grass; in jade towers, revelers lie drunk beneath skies bright with apricot blossoms.

u.src: One day, Wang Qing entered the government office at the fifth watch to answer the morning roll call. When his duties were done, he strolled out through the southern gate and went sightseeing in the Yujin Gardens.
This was in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era under Emperor Huizong.

It was mid-spring. Sightseers swarmed like ants and mounted soldiers massed like clouds. Just so: In the imperial gardens flowers bloom and willows doze beside the dikes; among the throngs of pleasure-seekers mingle lovely women.
Horses with golden bridles neigh upon the fragrant grass; in jade towers, revelers lie drunk beneath skies bright with apricot blossoms.

p.src: After amusing himself alone for a while, Wang Qing leaned one shoulder against a weeping willow beside a pond in the gardens, intending to wait for an acquaintance so that they might go together to a wineshop, drink a few cups, and then return to the city. Before long, he saw some ten stewards, guards, attendants, nurses, and others on the north side of the pond, surrounding a sedan chair in which sat a young woman as lovely as a flower. The young woman wished to admire the scenery and therefore had no bamboo blind lowered. Wang Qing was exceedingly fond of women. At the sight of such a beautiful young lady, his very soul seemed to be drawn from his body. He recognized the stewards and guards as men from the household of Tong Guan, Commissioner of Military Affairs. Wang Qing followed the sedan chair at a distance and trailed the party all the way to Genyue. Genyue stood in the northeastern corner of the capital and had been built by the Daoist Emperor. It contained more strange peaks and wondrous rocks, ancient trees and rare birds, pavilions, terraces, ponds, and halls than could be counted. Outside were vermilion walls and crimson gates resembling the entrances to the imperial precincts, guarded by palace eunuchs and imperial troops. Ordinary people dared not set so much as a toe before the gate. The party set down the sedan chair, and a nurse helped the young woman alight. Graceful and alluring, she swayed elegantly as she walked straight through the gate of Genyue. The imperial guards and eunuchs at the gate opened a path and allowed her to enter.

p.src: It turned out that the young woman was the daughter of Tong Guan’s younger brother, Tong Shi, and the granddaughter of Yang Jian. Tong Guan had raised her as his own daughter and betrothed her to Cai You’s son, making her Cai Jing’s future granddaughter-in-law. Her childhood name was Jiaoxiu, and she was sixteen years old. Having obtained Tong Guan’s permission, she took advantage of the emperor’s spending two days amusing himself at Li Shishi’s house and set out to visit Genyue. Tong Guan had given orders to the imperial guards and attendants beforehand, so none dared bar her way. Jiaoxiu had been inside for four hours, yet still had not emerged. That scoundrel Wang Qing waited outside in a daze until hunger gnawed at him. He wandered to a tavern on East Street, bought some wine and meat, and hastily downed six or seven cups. Fearing the woman might leave, he did not even settle the bill, but felt in his purse, pulled out a piece of silver weighing two qian, tossed it to the waiter, and said, “I’ll be back shortly to settle the account.” Wang Qing hurried back to the front of Genyue and waited a while longer. Presently the young woman appeared with her nurse, emerging from Genyue with dainty, measured steps. Instead of entering her sedan chair at once, she paused to admire the scenery outside the gardens. When Wang Qing edged forward to look at her, he found her truly exquisite. A lyric to the tune “Dragon Roiling the River” bears witness:

p.src: Graceful in form, endowed with surpassing beauty—what golden bower could be worthy to shelter her? A tiny mouth like a touched cherry, twin eyes filled with autumn waters. Had the bright new moon not risen clear last night, how could the tune of Little Liangzhou break my heart this morning? Fragrant and graceful, a peer of orchid and sweet grass; perfume drifts from her elegant hibiscus sleeves. In both their hearts, the restless ape of desire is snared by the moon’s lure and the flower’s hook.

u.src: Graceful in form, endowed with surpassing beauty—what golden bower could be worthy to shelter her?
A tiny mouth like a touched cherry, twin eyes filled with autumn waters.
Had the bright new moon not risen clear last night, how could the tune of Little Liangzhou break my heart this morning?

Fragrant and graceful, a peer of orchid and sweet grass; perfume drifts from her elegant hibiscus sleeves. In both their hearts, the restless ape of desire is snared by the moon’s lure and the flower’s hook.

p.src: As Wang Qing gazed upon her charms, his heart began to leap like a frightened deer; his bones went soft and his sinews numb. He was like a lion made of snow brought near a fire, half melted in an instant. From amid the crowd, Jiaoxiu stole a glance at Wang Qing’s appearance: phoenix eyes and thick, painted brows, a faint moustache, fair skin, and rosy cheeks. His crown was level, his brow broad and full, and his seven-foot frame was powerfully built. Skilled at stealing fragrance and pilfering jade, he was well versed in flirtation and illicit affairs. He stood before her, staring and lost in thought, handsome, dashing, and full of charm.

From amid the crowd, Jiaoxiu stole a glance at Wang Qing’s appearance: phoenix eyes and thick, painted brows, a faint moustache, fair skin, and rosy cheeks.
His crown was level, his brow broad and full, and his seven-foot frame was powerfully built.

p.src: At a single glance Jiaoxiu saw how dashing Wang Qing was, and she too took a liking to him. The stewards and guards shouted for the crowd to clear the way, and the nurse helped Jiaoxiu into her sedan chair. Surrounded by her retinue, she wound east and west until she reached the Temple of the Sacred Peak outside the Suanzao Gate, where she had come to burn incense. Wang Qing followed them to the temple. It was packed like mountains and seas of people, and he could not squeeze through; but when the crowd saw that the men were guards and stewards from Privy Councillor Tong’s household, they opened a path. Jiaoxiu alighted to offer incense. Wang Qing pushed and twisted his way forward, but could not get near her. Fearing rebuke from her attendants, he pretended to be an old acquaintance of the temple keeper and helped him light candles and burn incense, while his eyes never ceased sliding toward Jiaoxiu; she, in turn, repeatedly stole glances at him. Now Cai You’s son had been a simpleton from birth. At home Jiaoxiu had several times heard the matchmakers confirm that this was true, and day and night she lamented the injustice and seethed with resentment. Now that she had seen how handsome and dashing Wang Qing was, the little minx’s amorous heart was stirred. Among Tong’s household was a Guard Dong, who had already noticed what was happening and recognized Wang Qing, the rank-and-file soldier. Guard Dong struck Wang Qing square across the face and shouted, “Do you know whose lady this is? You are merely a common soldier of Kaifeng Prefecture. What brazen nerve you have, shoving and squeezing about here! Wait until I report you to His Excellency—then we shall see whether that donkey’s head of yours stays fast upon your neck!” Wang Qing dared not utter a sound. Covering his head, he fled like a rat and rushed out through the temple gate. He spat and cried, “Damn it! How could I be such a fool! How could a mangy toad ever dream of eating swan’s flesh?” That evening he swallowed his anger and returned home in shame. Little did he know that after Jiaoxiu returned to the mansion, she thought of him day and night. She lavishly bribed her maid, who in turn questioned Guard Dong and had him tell her all about Wang Qing. The maid was acquainted with an old woman named Xue. Together they acted as go-betweens, secretly luring Wang Qing in through the back gate. Unseen by man or ghost, he began an affair with Jiaoxiu. That scoundrel Wang Qing was beside himself with joy and spent every day drinking.

p.src: Time slipped by, and three months passed. But joy at its height gives birth to sorrow. One day Wang Qing got drunk as mud and let the secret slip before Zhang Bin, a regular soldier of the prefecture. The affair was soon noised abroad and inevitably reached Tong Guan’s ears. Tong Guan flew into a rage and began scheming to find some charge by which to have Wang Qing sent away, but of that there is no need to speak for now.

p.src: Now let us speak of Wang Qing. Since the affair had come to light, he no longer dared enter Tong’s mansion. One day he sat idly at home. It was already late in the fifth month, and the weather was sweltering. Wang Qing carried a bench into the courtyard to cool himself. Just as he rose and went indoors to fetch a fan, he saw the bench move on its four legs and walk in from the courtyard. Wang Qing shouted, “What sorcery is this!” He whipped up his right foot and gave the bench a single kick. Wang Qing cried out, “Oh, the pain!” Had he not kicked it, all would have been well; but the moment he did, misfortune came upon him. Truly, heaven sends storms without warning, and fortune or calamity may befall a man between dawn and dusk. Why did Wang Qing cry out in pain when he kicked the bench? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
